To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) activation of central opioid-receptors initiates the decompensated phase of hemorrhage-induced hypotension, and 2), the effective dose of opioid agonists is likely to activate mu-opioid-receptors.
activation of central opioid-receptors determines the timing of decompensation during acute hemorrhage in conscious, unrestrained sheep.
naloxone delays the decompensational phase of hemorrhage and increases the hemorrhage volume needed before MAP falls to 50 mm Hg, while morphine decreases this hemorrhage volume.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the central regulation of cardiovascular function and blood volume homeostasis in the conscious sheep.
the central regulation of blood pressure in conscious sheep during hypovolemia induced by acute hemorrhage.
the role of central opioid receptors in the regulation of blood pressure in conscious animals and humans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
endogenous opioid-receptor activation delays decompensation in hemorrhage-induced hypotension in conscious sheep, but the mechanism by which it does this remains unknown.

the decompensating phase of acute hemorrhage-induced hemorrhagic shock in conscious sheep is initiated by activation of opioid receptors located in the brain, but the exact location of these receptors and their precise role in the initiation of decompensation remain to be established.
central opioid receptors play a role in the decompensated phase, but they are not the only mechanism involved.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the endogenous activation of opioid receptors is not involved in the initiation of the decompensation phase of hemorrhage.
the decompensating phase in sheep is not due to activation of opioid receptors.
the decompensated phase of hemorrhage is initiated by the activation of central opioid receptor and the decompensating mechanism can be blocked by the activation of mu-opioid receptor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
central opioid receptors play a role in the decompensation phase of hemorrhage.
opioid receptors in the CNS are involved in the decompensated phase of hemorrhagic shock.
central opioid receptor activation is a major factor in the initiation of the decompensation phase of hemorrhagic hypovolemia.
